lessons.title: क्या …? (kyā …?) — the yes-or-no question
lessons.gloss: the same क्या you know as what, moved to the front, where it means nothing at all and asks a yes-or-no question

segments.text: Retrieve the two items before this one by name: -कर and जब … तब. Then say हाँ and नहीं — two answers with no question.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: क्या at the FRONT means nothing

segments.text: क्या आप कल आ सकते हैं? — kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ? — Can you come tomorrow?
Put क्या at the very front and it stops meaning what: it marks the sentence as a yes-or-no question and nothing else moves, because Hindi cannot invert the way English does with can you.
Position is the whole difference:
आप क्या कर सकते हैं? — what can you do? — inside.
क्या आप आ सकते हैं? (āp ā sakte haiṁ?) — can you come? — in front.
Answer either with हाँ or नहीं. A language that cannot invert reaches for a particle; Persian and Russian do the same.

segments.instruction: kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ? and answer — hāṁ or nahīṁ
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ?* and answer — *hāṁ* or *nahīṁ*]

segments.instruction: the pair — āp kyā kar sakte haiṁ? / kyā āp ā sakte haiṁ?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the pair — *āp kyā kar sakte haiṁ?* / *kyā āp ā sakte haiṁ?*]

segments.prompt: Say the two kya questions back to back: what can you do, and can you come.
acceptedResponses: āp kyā kar sakte haiṁ? — kyā āp ā sakte haiṁ?
आप क्या कर सकते हैं? क्या आप आ सकते हैं?

feedback.correct: Inside it means what; in front it means nothing.
feedback.incorrect: Move kyā to the very front and it stops meaning what.

segments.text: What does क्या mean at the very front? (Nothing — it marks a yes-or-no question.) What else moves? (Nothing.)
Sources: Wiktionary: क्या.

lessons.title: The question that is only a voice
lessons.gloss: the rising voice — how a Hindi yes-or-no question is asked when no क्या is there, which is most of the time

segments.text: Say क्या आप आ सकते हैं? (āp ā sakte haiṁ?) — the question you got one lesson ago. Now say it again and leave the first word out.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: the rise carries it alone

segments.text: आप आ सकते हैं? — āp ā sakte haiṁ? — Can you come?

Word for word that is a statement. What makes it a question is the pitch of the last two syllables going up, and nothing else. Speakers drop क्या far more often than they use it, so this is the ordinary form and the particle is the careful one.
Say the pair and listen, do not read:
आप आ सकते हैं. — flat at the end — you can come.
आप आ सकते हैं? (āp ā sakte haiṁ?) — rising at the end — can you come?

Two things follow. First, you can ask any yes-or-no question in Hindi today without learning another word — every statement in this book is already a question if you lift the end of it. Second, and less comfortable: a listening paper will hand you the rise without the particle, so the ear has to catch it. A candidate reading only for क्या will hear a statement and answer nothing.

segments.instruction: āp ā sakte haiṁ. flat, then āp ā sakte haiṁ? rising
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *āp ā sakte haiṁ.* flat, then *āp ā sakte haiṁ?* rising]

segments.instruction: the same sentence with the particle — kyā āp ā sakte haiṁ?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the same sentence with the particle — *kyā āp ā sakte haiṁ?*]

segments.instruction: which of the three a Hindi speaker uses most — the rise
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the three a Hindi speaker uses most — **the rise**]

segments.prompt: Say the same four words twice — as a statement, then as a question — and name what changed.
acceptedResponses: āp ā sakte haiṁ. / āp ā sakte haiṁ? — only the pitch at the end
आप आ सकते हैं. आप आ सकते हैं? the rise

feedback.correct: Same words; the voice does all the work.
feedback.incorrect: Nothing in the words changes — lift the last two syllables.

segments.text: What turns आप आ सकते हैं into a question with no extra word? (The pitch rising at the end.) Which form do speakers use more often, that or क्या? (The rise.)

lessons.title: … है ना? (… hai nā?) — "isn't it?"
lessons.gloss: the confirmation tag — one syllable on the end of a sentence you already own

segments.text: क्या at the front asks something you do not know. Often you DO know, and want it confirmed. Different move, different word, other end.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: hanging a check on the end

segments.text: चाय ठीक है ना? — chāy ṭhīk hai nā? — The tea is fine, isn't it?
Take any statement you can make, put ना on the end, and it becomes a check: you say what you believe and invite the listener to agree. The answer comes back as हाँ or नहीं.
Set the two questions side by side:
क्या चाय ठीक है? — is the tea fine? — I do not know.
चाय ठीक है ना? — the tea is fine, isn't it? — I think so; agree with me.
Use the tag when you mean the particle and you have claimed to know the answer already.

One syllable buys a whole conversational turn: every sentence in this book is now something you can offer for agreement. The tag is the old negative न used as an invitation — a negative asking for a yes, exactly as English does in isn't it? and Marathi with the same syllable.

segments.instruction: chāy ṭhīk hai nā? then answer yourself — hāṁ
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *chāy ṭhīk hai nā?* then answer yourself — *hāṁ*]

segments.instruction: the pair — kyā chāy ṭhīk hai? / chāy ṭhīk hai nā?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the pair — *kyā chāy ṭhīk hai?* / *chāy ṭhīk hai nā?*]

segments.instruction: which one already believes the answer — the tag
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which one already believes the answer — **the tag**]

segments.prompt: Ask whether the tea is fine two ways: not knowing, then expecting agreement.
acceptedResponses: kyā chāy ṭhīk hai? — chāy ṭhīk hai nā?
क्या चाय ठीक है? चाय ठीक है ना?

feedback.correct: Particle at the front, tag at the end.
feedback.incorrect: kyā goes in front and asks; nā goes on the end and expects a yes.

segments.text: What does ना on the end of a statement do? (Asks the listener to confirm it.) How is that different from क्या at the front? (क्या does not know the answer; ना expects agreement.)
Sources: Wiktionary: ना.

lessons.title: Everything that joins, and everything that asks
lessons.gloss: every joining word and every question shape in the book, run once

segments.text: Seven chapters ago you could name a thousand Hindi things and say nothing about two of them at once. Name the three joiners this run opened with, and say where the verb of each half goes.
Say each of the four, and after each one name what the underneath clause is doing: a content, a reason, a time, a sequence.

segments.prompt: Say four sentences with a clause underneath: a reported thought, a reason, a when-frame, and a chained pair.
acceptedResponses: maiṁ sochtā hūṁ ki chāy ṭhīk hai; maiṁ kal nahīṁ ā saktā kyoṁki maiṁ kām kartā hūṁ; jab maiṁ hindī boltā hūṁ, tab āp sunte haiṁ; maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ
मैं सोचता हूँ कि चाय ठीक है. मैं कल नहीं आ सकता क्योंकि मैं काम करता हूँ. जब मैं हिंदी बोलता हूँ, तब आप सुनते हैं. मैं किताब देखकर आता हूँ

feedback.correct: Content, reason, time, sequence — four ways to put one clause under another.
feedback.incorrect: Run them in order: ki, kyoṁki, jab...tab, -kar.

segments.instruction: kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ? — you do not know
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kyā āp kal ā sakte haiṁ?* — you do not know]

segments.instruction: chāy ṭhīk hai nā? — you think you do
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *chāy ṭhīk hai nā?* — you think you do]

segments.instruction: āp kab ā sakte haiṁ?, āp kyoṁ nahīṁ ā sakte?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *āp kab ā sakte haiṁ?* · *āp kyoṁ nahīṁ ā sakte?*]

segments.instruction: āp kal ā sakte haiṁ? with no particle at all, on a rising voice
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *āp kal ā sakte haiṁ?* with no particle at all, on a rising voice]

segments.text: Which joining words treat the two halves as EQUALS? (aur, या, लेकिन.) Which ones put one half UNDERNEATH the other? (कि, क्योंकि, जब … तब, -कर.) And which single word means what in the middle of a sentence and nothing at all at the front? (क्या.) Then stop.
